items.title: Senior Research Associate in Infectious Disease Epidemiology (1224-26)
items.description:
We are seeking to appoint a full-time Research Associate or Senior Research Associate  until March 2029, with the possibility of further extension.  This is an exciting opportunity to join a growing research programme using real-world contact data and mathematical modelling to understand how infectious diseases spread and the potential impact of different control measures. The work will focus predominantly on two uniquely rich datasets, one capturing general population contact patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic using large-scale contact tracing data, and one focused specifically on school-aged children, to help shape public health policy on disease control both in schools and more broadly. The successful candidate will join Lancaster Medical School and work closely with Dr Jonathan Read and Dr Trystan Leng.  We welcome applications from researchers with a PhD in (or equivalent experience) in infectious disease epidemiology, mathematical modelling, quantitative social science, or a related discipline. The postholder will clean and analyse contact patterns from two distinct datasets: 1) the NHS/UKHSA contact tracing data from England, collected during the COVID-19 pandemic and 2) data collected from the School and Community Connections study, a bespoke study which will collect data specifically for this analysis, aimed at understanding the contact patterns of schoolchildren. Further, the postholder will use transmission-dynamic models informed by this contact data alongside surveillance data, fitted using Bayesian methods, to undertake scenario-based mathematical modelling of the potential impact of a range of public health interventions, as well as exploring the usefulness of contact data in explaining observed patterns of incidence.  Depending on experience, the postholder may also contribute to survey design and data collection during the School and Community Connections Study.  The post is funded jointly through a MRC grant awarded to Dr Read and through Dr Leng's Wellcome Early Career Award 'Control without closure: school-level approaches for pathogen control within and between schools':  https://wellcome.org/research-funding/funding-portfolio/funded-grants/control-without-closure-school-level-approaches   You will liaise with colleagues within Lancaster Medical School (Dr Sam Moore) alongside external partners, including Prof Henrik Salje (University of Cambridge), Prof Moritz Kraemer (University of Oxford), colleagues at UKHSA, and the UK government’s Department for Education science team.  You will be expected to be based at Lancaster University, however, we can consider remote working within the UK. There is also the opportunity for a longer-term research visit to external partners’ institutions.  We welcome applications from candidates seeking flexible working requests.  You will join a top 10-UK university in the Complete University Guide 2027 situated in a vibrant research environment. Lancaster Medical School, within the Faculty of Health and Medicine (FHM) at Lancaster University, provides a friendly research environment that strongly supports the individual needs of each employee and which actively promotes a healthy work-life balance. FHM is committed to family-friendly and flexible working policies and has held a Silver Athena SWAN award since 2014 in recognition of its good employment practice undertaken to address gender equality in higher education and research.  For more information, please contact:  Dr Jonathan Read:  Jonathan.read@lancaster.ac.uk   Dr Trystan Leng,  t.leng@lancaster.ac.uk   The post is available from 1 st  January 2027.

items.title: Senior / Research Associate in Plant Biochemistry (1140-26)
items.description:
Job Title: Senior/ Research Associate in Plant Biochemistry   Contract: Indefinite with end date (currently 31/08/2028)   Position Summary:   Applications are invited for a postdoctoral researcher in Plant Biochemistry within the  Lancaster Photosynthesis team  under the supervision of Dr Doug Orr. This new position will join the Plant Biology grouping within the Lancaster Environment Centre, which consists of roughly 35 people including PIs, postdoctoral researchers, research technicians and postgraduate students.  This is part of a BBSRC-funded project that focuses on improving our understanding of Rubisco activity, and pursuing a novel target for increasing Rubisco activity in plants and cyanobacteria. This project is in collaboration with Prof. Martin Cann at Durham University. At Lancaster we will focus on understanding Rubisco activity of recombinant proteins  in vitro , and testing these  in planta  to understand the impact of mutations on leaf level photosynthesis.  The ideal candidate for this position in Plant Biochemistry will have a genuine interest and the curiosity to pursue new research avenues in Rubisco. With training and support, you will be responsible for leading  in vitro  and  in vivo  research to advance the understanding of Rubisco activity. You will lead the molecular and biochemical study of novel Rubisco variants to build fundamental understanding, and lead the physiological characterisation of plants expressing these proteins. You will design and carry out experimental and computational work, analyse data, present results in oral and written form and lead the preparation of scientific manuscripts.  You will join the collaborative and supportive  Lancaster Photosynthesis team  and have access to state-of-the-art resources, including a well-equipped lab for plant molecular biology and biochemistry work using ionising radiation, high-specification plant growth chambers, and the Lancaster High End Computing (HEC) Cluster. Professional development opportunities and training courses to broaden your expertise and skills will be encouraged and are covered by the project.  Individuals from all diversity groups are encouraged to apply. LEC offers a collegial and stimulating environment for career development, based on departmental values and embedded Equality, Diversity and Inclusivity (EDI) considerations and actions. We are committed to family-friendly and flexible working policies on an individual basis, as well as the Athena SWAN Charter, which recognises and celebrates good employment practice undertaken to address gender equality in higher education and research. Furthermore, we are active and progressive around sustainability, wellbeing and social justice agendas.      Timeframe:   This position is available for immediate start, with candidates ideally available to start by early 2027, however this is negotiable.  You will join us on an indefinite contract however the role remains contingent on external funding. This position will initially have an end date of 30/08/2028, with the possibility for extension.  We anticipate interviews will be held within 3 weeks of the closing date, with decisions communicated 1-2 weeks after the interview date.      To apply for this post:   In reading your application documents, we are assessing if you are a good fit to this position and if this position is a good fit for you. To be able to do this, we need you to tell us about your expertise and experience to date, and your research interests. We want to know about the skills you had the opportunity to develop, put within the context of your previous study/work environment by, for example, briefly describing the research facilities available to you, and whether you had opportunities to attend conferences/scientific meetings and develop transferable skills. Please let us know if you have had a career break for any reason so that we can consider the achievements listed on your CV, including your publication record, in relation to these factors.   There is flexibility to appoint either a junior (grade 6) or senior (grade 7) postdoc to this role, with responsibilities and salary set accordingly, and dependent on the successful candidate’s current expertise and experience level.      What to include in each section of your application?    Cover letter:  Please discuss why you are interested in this position, your career goals, and how you anticipate this position will help you achieve those goals. Please also describe the skills you have developed that are relevant to this post and tell us about any skills you want to develop further. It is helpful for us to know your contribution toward the achievements and experiences listed on your CV that are relevant to this post.   CV:  Please include the following sections: Scientific interests; Education history; Professional experience/Employment history; Areas of expertise/Skills; Publications; Presentations.  And, if applicable: Honours/Awards/Prizes/Funding (e.g. travel grant, best poster); Academic service (e.g. review of manuscripts); Outreach; Career development (e.g. training courses or workshops).   Supporting Statements:  Please provide a supporting statement for each criterium in the Personal Specification document that is listed as being scored via “Supporting Statements”. This should include examples that provide evidence of your experience and expertise. Aim for one paragraph per criterium (~50-200 words).   Referees:  Contact information for at least two referees.      For informal enquiries relating to this post, please contact:   Dr Doug Orr  d.j.orr@lancaster.ac.uk .  Further details on our research and team are available here:   http://wp.lancs.ac.uk/lancsphotosynthesis/    https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/lec/about-us/people/douglas-orr

items.title: Senior Research Associate (1137-26)
items.description:
The School of Mathematical Sciences at Lancaster University invites applications for a three-year postdoctoral position to work on the EPSRC-funded project  “ Mutations and geometric models”. The Principal Investigator is Dr Coelho Simões.   Calabi-Yau (CY) triangulated categories are ubiquitous in mathematics, particularly in geometry and representation theory. Due to their physical origin, n-CY categories have been extensively studied for n=2,3. However, as a homological condition, the n-CY property can be studied for any integer n meaning there are many more examples: categories naturally arising in modular representation theory, singularity theory, Fuss-Catalan combinatorics, and higher homological algebra are n-CY for n different from 2 and 3. The systematic study of CY categories in these wider contexts is in its infancy and many aspects remain poorly understood. The main aim of the project seeks to provide methods to address this shortfall using mutations and geometric models.  The successful candidate is expected to hold a PhD degree in mathematics or a related discipline, with specialism in one of the fields of homological algebra, representation theory or algebraic combinatorics. Expertise in triangulated categories, representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, combinatorial/geometric models arising from surfaces, singularity theory or modular representation theory is highly desirable. You will be expected to learn quickly, engage with new ideas, and contribute new insights.  This work will take place in our thriving Pure Mathematics section, which has considerable expertise in algebra, geometry, analysis, probability, and discrete mathematics. Lancaster is one of the UK’s top mathematical science departments, ranked 7th in the most recent Research Excellence Framework, and joint 1st for the impact of its research. The School, which holds an Athena SWAN Bronze Award, strives to provide a supportive and friendly environment for early career researchers, and offers a comprehensive career development programme. You will be able to focus on your research as the post carries no teaching or administrative duties. Teaching experience will be available on a voluntary basis should you wish to gain teaching experience. You will be encouraged to conduct research visits and will have access to travel funds to do so.   The position starts on 1st February 2027 (or as soon as possible after), for up to 36 months. When applying, in addition to completing the online application, candidates should attach a full CV, a cover letter, a 1-page research statement describing how your expertise is relevant to this position and your future research plans, and the details of two referees. Interviews will take place in December and will be conducted online.  Please contact Dr Raquel Coelho Simões (   r.coelhosimoes@lancaster.ac.uk ) for further information or to discuss the post informally.

This will include assuming responsibilities for informatics- and computational-led data analysis to identify new opportunities via market analysis, drug repurposing/discovery, formal knowledge representation, and precision medicine-led biomarker discovery to complement new therapeutic veterinary medicine approaches.    This work is contextualised into a programme award from our sponsors Zoetis (the largest animal health corporation globally) that seeks to support their interests in key disease issues. The post will thus involve collaborative working with industry partners, charities, as well as other universities and research institutes across the UK and internationally. The job holder will develop, repurpose and use new research techniques and methods, in consultation with the research supervisor and with input from Zoetis employees. These studies will include assessing interview and stakeholder data for unmet need definition, in-silico drug repurposing and trial research, critical evaluation and interpretation of biomarker discovery datasets (and in particular proteomics and transcriptomics), plus extensive library research.   The overall programme of research will be jointly developed by Prof. Nophar Geifman and the person appointed. There are opportunities to broaden out into other areas such as new algorithm development, and advanced computational methodologies for integrated analyses.    About you   You will have a key role in planning, designing and executing a range of analyses on varied novel projects aimed at high-impact and theoretically valuable research questions. Strong quantitative research skills with hands-on real-world experience are essential. You must have experience in the application of informatics pipelines to health and biomedical data (outside educational settings). items.description:
The University of Surrey is a global community of ideas and people, dedicated to life-changing education and research.   We are ambitious and have a bold vision of what we want to achieve - shaping ourselves into one of the best universities in the world, which we are achieving through the talents and endeavour of every employee.    Our culture empowers people to achieve this aim and to collectively, and individually, make a real difference.    The role  Spatial abilities include the ability to understand the spatial properties of objects and to mentally visualise objects and problems. Spatial abilities in childhood predict adult expertise in STEM, and spatial training has been shown to be effective in improving children’s mathematics competence. This project is a partnership between Prof. Emily Farran, Director of the Cognition, Genes and Developmental Variability (CoGDeV) lab (lead unit), an internationally recognised centre for spatial-mathematics research and impact, Dr. Cath Gripton, Associate Director of the Observatory for Mathematical Education, Dr. Sue Gifford, Chair of the Early Childhood Maths Group and Chair of the Royal Society's Advisory Committee on Mathematics Education Primary and Early Years Expert Panel, and Prof. Camilla Gilmore, Director of the ESRC Centre for Early Mathematics Learning.   Drawing on our existing ECMG Spatial Reasoning Toolkit, a set of professional development resources developed for practitioners working with young children, you will be part of a team completing a Randomised Control Trial of the ECMG Spatial Reasoning Toolkit targeted at 3- to 4-year-olds and their nursery settings. Your primary role is to support engagement and recruitment of nursery settings to the programme. This involves following an engagement, marketing and recruitment plan, building networks, engaging stakeholders, creating and organising engagement materials such a webinars, recruitment flyers and social media advertising, and keeping a recruitment log. You will also support the wider team in the development of intervention material and in planning the intervention phase of the project.  This is a fixed-term post starting in March 2027 and running until September 2027.  About you  You will be part of a strong team of experts in spatial cognition and mathematical learning at the interface between research and practice. You will have a BSc or equivalent qualification in Psychology or a related subject. You will be a strong team member with excellent communication and organisational skills, experience of supporting engagement or recruitment activities and in following research protocols.   An Enhanced DBS check is required for this position.  How to apply  To apply, please submit your CV & cover letter via the University website.  You are welcome to contact Prof. Emily Farran ( e.farran@surrey.ac.uk ) if you would like further information or to discuss the post.

items.description:
The University of Surrey is a global community of ideas and people, dedicated to life-changing education and research.   We are ambitious and have a bold vision of what we want to achieve - shaping ourselves into one of the best universities in the world, which we are achieving through the talents and endeavour of every employee.    Our culture empowers people to achieve this aim and to collectively, and individually, make a real difference.    The role  The University of Surrey has recently been awarded a three-year project by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council. The title of the project is Spectrally Efficient Low Cost Energy Efficient Communication for Transport using 3D Angular Modes (SELECT-3DAM). We are seeking a Research Fellow to join us for the remainder of the project (expected until March 2029) on a full-time basis.  This work builds on recent seminal work carried out by the project investigators on Linear Angular Momentum Multiplexing (LAMM). The project is an exciting opportunity to undertake work on antenna synthesis and physical layer radio to underpin the science to enable practical implementation of an evolution of this concept, 3D Angular Momentum Multiplexing (3DAMM), for advanced infrastructure to train communications.   Its application is to provide a low cost, energy efficient solution to deliver reliable gigabit connectivity to train carriages in tunnels. 3DAMM is a highly innovative wireless transmission architecture that has promise of revolutionising spectral efficiency in some wireless links.   We are looking to attract the brightest and best to form an effective team to develop and investigate the concept further. Together with another researcher appointed to the role focused on RF and antennas, this will include designing and constructing a concept demonstrator.  The postholder will undertake a range of research activities within a specified research area in infrastructure to train communications by means of 3D Angular Momentum Multiplexing, assuming responsibility for specific areas of projects and making use of new research techniques and methods, in consultation with the research award holder or supervisor. This will include computer-based simulations, library research, critical evaluation and interpretation as well as assisting other researchers with practical measurements. Join the University of Southampton as a Doctoral Candidate within DECODES: Deciphering the Splicing Code in Human Disease, a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Network funded through Horizon Europe. You will undertake interdisciplinary doctoral research at the interface of rare disease genomics, RNA biology and computational analysis, while benefiting from advanced training, transferable-skills development and collaboration across an international network spanning academia, clinical research and industry.   The role    Your project will investigate how long-read DNA sequencing, RNA sequencing and methylation profiling can improve diagnosis for people with unresolved rare diseases. You will also explore artificial intelligence and machine-learning approaches for integrating multi-omic datasets and identifying disease-causing variants and potential RNA therapeutic targets.  Working within DECODES, you will contribute to high-quality, reproducible research and communicate findings through network activities, publications and conferences. The role requires engagement with collaborators across Europe and willingness to travel and relocate internationally for planned research secondments. The University of Southampton aims to create an environment where everyone can thrive and fosters inclusion, respect and equality of opportunity. items.title: Research Fellow in Polar Oceanography (3550926HN)
items.description:
We are seeking an enthusiastic Research Fellow to join our vibrant research community at the National Oceanography Centre Southampton, University of Southampton, to work on the European Research Council-funded ROSS-SHIFT (Ross Sea Regime Shift) project.  The successful candidate will investigate potential regime shifts in ocean circulation in the Ross Sea and wider Southern Ocean, and their implications for Antarctic Ice Sheet melting and the Southern Ocean Overturning Circulation. The research will aim to improve our understanding of how changes in ocean circulation and freshwater content influence ocean heat transport towards Antarctic ice shelves, affect their basal melting, and interact with the large-scale overturning circulation. The work will involve the analysis of satellite observations, alongside in situ oceanographic measurements and numerical model outputs, to identify, characterise, and understand changes in Southern Ocean dynamics.  This position offers an exciting opportunity to contribute to cutting-edge Antarctic research in an international, collaborative environment, with the possibility of participating in Antarctic research cruises. The successful candidate will work closely with collaborators at the British Antarctic Survey, University College London, the University of Gothenburg, the Norwegian Polar Institute and the University of Naples Parthenope.  We welcome applications from researchers with experience in physical oceanography, satellite remote sensing, ocean observations, numerical modelling, or related disciplines such as mathematics and physics.  The position is expected to start on 1 March 2027 for an initial period of two years, with the possibility of extension subject to satisfactory progress and funding availability. Some flexibility regarding the start date is available and can be discussed with the successful candidate. For further information or informal enquiries, please contact Dr Alessandro Silvano  a.silvano@soton.ac.uk . items.title: Research Fellow in Global Marine Ecosystem Modelling (3551126HN)
items.description:
We have an exciting opportunity for a postdoctoral researcher to investigate how phytoplankton physiology influences ocean carbon cycling. The successful candidate will join a UK-US research project, From Monod to Macromolecules: assessing nutrient-carbon coupling in a hierarchy of ocean-ecosystem models, based at the University of Southampton and working in collaboration with researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).  The project will compare different approaches to representing phytoplankton physiology within the MITgcm-Darwin ocean ecosystem model. The successful candidate will implement and evaluate a range of physiological sub-models with the MIT virtual ocean environment, to investigate which aspects of cellular physiology are important for predicting nutrient cycling, primary production and carbon export.  The work will involve developing and testing numerical models, running global ocean simulations and analysing model outputs alongside oceanographic observations. There will also be opportunities to investigate how the effects of physiological complexity depend on environmental variability and ecological interactions.  We are looking for someone with strong quantitative and programming skills, and experience developing or analysing numerical models. A background in marine ecology, oceanography, biogeochemistry, applied mathematics or a related field would be beneficial. Experience with Fortran, high-performance computing and/or marine ecosystem models would be advantageous, but is not essential.  At Southampton, you will work closely with Dr Ben Ward and Professor Mark Moore, in collaboration with Professor Mick Follows, Dr Stephanie Dutkiewicz and colleagues at MIT. You will also have opportunities to work with staff and students across the wider Marine Biogeochemistry research group and the School of Ocean and Earth Science at the University of Southampton. The successful candidate will be expected to contribute to the publication of research findings in peer-reviewed journals and to present their work at national and international scientific conferences.  We welcome applications from all candidates with an interest in the role, and those who are committed to helping us create a diverse and inclusive work environment.  We encourage applications from candidates from Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic communities, people who identify as LGBTQ+ and people with disabilities. We recognise that employees may wish to have working patterns that fit with their caring responsibilities or work-life balance.  Due consideration will be given to applicants who have had career breaks for reasons including maternity, paternity or adoption leave, disability or illness. We offer a generous holiday allowance and additional University closure days, subsidised health and fitness facilities and access to the Universities Superannuation Scheme (USS).  Applications for Research Fellow positions will be considered from candidates who are working towards or nearing completion of a relevant PhD qualification.   The position is full-time and fixed-term for 20 months, with an anticipated start in early 2027.   For informal enquiries, please contact Dr Ben Ward ( b.a.ward@soton.ac.uk ). Be a part of the University of Southampton, an institution in the top one per cent of world universities and one of the UK’s Russell group research-intensive universities. We have an international reputation for research, teaching and enterprise activities. You will work in the world leading Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC) and will have access to the world class facilities and dedicated researchers that this provides. The Telecommunications Systems Laboratory is equipped with state-of-the-art equipment for experimentation in photonic systems and provides direct access to the UK’s National Dark Fibre Facility, a unique geographically distributed transmission facility dedicated to research, linking together four top British universities. items.title: Research Fellow in Cell and Developmental Biology (3545826BJ)
items.description:
We are seeking a motivated and enthusiastic Research Fellow to join the Salah Elias laboratory at the University of Southampton and lead the experimental research within a BBSRC-funded project investigating mechanisms of mammary epithelial morphogenesis through AI-integrated human organoid models and predictive cell fate mapping. This is an excellent opportunity to shape an innovative project and develop a distinctive interdisciplinary profile at the interface of cell and developmental biology, human organoid models, advanced imaging, molecular phenotyping and computational biology.   About the project   The project combines patient-derived mammary organoids, high-resolution 3D/4D imaging, single-cell transcriptomics and AI-driven analysis and modelling to uncover mechanisms governing epithelial morphogenesis. At its core is a fundamental question: how do polarised cell divisions coordinate luminogenesis with cell fate and differentiation to build and maintain functional epithelial architecture? By addressing this question in physiologically relevant human models, the project aims to define how these mechanisms safeguard epithelial integrity and how their disruption leads to abnormal tissue organisation.  You will take a central role in the scientific development of this ambitious programme, including experimental design, data analysis and interpretation. You will use patient-derived human mammary organoids and gene loss-of-function approaches, together with high-resolution 3D/4D fluorescence imaging, fate mapping, advanced quantitative analysis, and single-cell RNA sequencing, to connect molecular and cellular mechanisms with cell fate and tissue architecture.  A major strength of the project is the integration of experimental and computational biology. Working with computational researchers, you will integrate multimodal imaging and transcriptomic data into AI-driven mechanistic and predictive models to determine how changes at the level of individual cells influence tissue-level organisation and function.   About you   You will have a PhD, or be close to completing one, in cell biology, developmental biology, stem cell biology or a related discipline.  You will have strong experimental experience across several relevant areas of cell and developmental biology, which may include organoid or mammalian cell culture, epithelial biology, high-resolution fluorescence microscopy and molecular biology. Experience in advanced automated or semi-automated quantitative image analysis would be particularly valuable. An understanding of computational or mathematical modelling would be advantageous, but is not essential.  You will be a creative and collaborative scientist with a proactive, analytical approach and enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research. You should be able to plan and conduct rigorous experiments, interpret data, troubleshoot methods and communicate findings clearly.  Alongside leading the experimental research, you will contribute scientific ideas and interpretation, support collaborative projects, help develop grant proposals, prepare research for publication in international peer-reviewed journals, train colleagues in new methods and advise on scientific protocols. You will bring excellent interpersonal skills and work constructively with colleagues and collaborators across disciplines.   What we offer   You will join a collaborative, multidisciplinary and supportive research environment bringing together expertise in mammary biology, organoids, advanced imaging, single-cell biology, AI and computational modelling. You will have access to state-of-the-art microscopy, flow-cytometry and high-performance computing facilities, multidisciplinary training and career-development opportunities.  The University of Southampton offers a range of benefits, including a generous holiday allowance and additional University closure days. We support flexible working and a healthy work–life balance, alongside access to the Universities Superannuation Scheme (USS), subsidised health and fitness facilities and a range of staff discounts.  The post is offered on a three-year fixed-term basis.  For informal enquiries, please contact Dr Salah Elias at  S.K.Elias@soton.ac.uk .

items.title: Research Fellow in Economic Early-warning Signals of Accelerated Climate Change and Earth-System Tipping Points (BUSAF1025)
items.description:
Overview of the Role   Are you a researcher with demonstrable expertise in the analysis of climatological data and the implementation and interpretation of climate model projections? Do you have a demonstrable interest in engaging with stakeholders, particularly in public policy and the financial sector? Do you have a background within climate science?    This project will address the lack of adequate early-warning systems for accelerated climate change and tipping-points, for the insurance sector and more broadly. It also aims to address an associated challenge for the insurance sector, given its criticality to the global economy, by helping the sector understand the stressors, and adaptation responses to those stressors, it is likely to face in the coming decades due to the combined effects of climate change, the transition to a net zero economy including regulatory challenges, and potential geopolitical threats.  Through this work, in collaboration with the insurance and reinsurance industry, the successful candidate will help to develop and test a novel early-warning system for accelerating climate change and tipping-points, with aim of informing policy and wider society that unmanageable levels of climate change, with different modalities of climate impacts, are approaching.  This approach draws on ideas from climate attribution and optimal fingerprinting and from economics signal detection but extends this through the application of social science techniques, including decision-gaming and reverse stress testing, by using the insurance sector as a filter to help detect the early signs of an accelerated climate change signal against the background noise of natural variability in the climate.  As part of this early-warning system development, we will produce multi-dimensional storylines using interdisciplinary teams to combine understanding on physical climate change, policy and regulatory changes linked to the net zero transition, and potential geopolitical impacts. These will be applicable to stress-testing in insurance, but with broader applications across finance as well as for government and other sectors aiming to adapt.  The successful candidate will also work closely with collaborators across the University (the Faculties of Business and Environment and Social Sciences) and with co-investigators at the University of Oxford to contribute to the development of cross-cutting underpinning methodological advancements, including new approaches to describing and characterising confidence levels, treatments of uncertainty in bringing together disparate data and models, approaches to characterising compounding and correlated risks, and tail-risk scenarios including tipping points. items.title: Research Fellow in Energy Geostructures (EPSCV1173)
items.description:
Heating and cooling of buildings is a key priority for global decarbonisation due to the scale of the demand and the current reliance on fossil fuels. Energy geostructures, where civil engineering substructures are connected to ground source heat pump systems offer a novel solution to this challenge. Appropriate design of energy geostructures requires consideration of the thermal behaviour and associated energy assessment. At the University of Leeds, our dynamic  energy geotechnics  team are leading research in this growing area. We would like to recruit someone to develop our research in design and analysis of diaphragm walls used for thermal energy extraction. Are you an ambitious researcher looking for a new challenge? Do you have expertise in ground energy systems and energy geostructures, especially their thermal analysis and design? Do you want to join an expanding research team at a leading UK university?  As part of an exciting  EPSRC-FAPESP project, Efficient Ground Energy Systems in Diaphragm Walls in Challenging Conditions , led by Prof Fleur Loveridge, you will lead innovative research into the design and analysis of energy retaining walls used as ground heat exchangers. The project aims to encourage the adoption of energy retaining walls through provision of better guidance. It includes a mixture of laboratory and field scale testing and a range of computational techniques carried out across three Universities – University of Leeds, University of Dundee and University of Sao Paulo. In particular the project will:    Understand the impact of temporary and spatial variation in ground properties on heat transfer and stress/strain conditions in the walls;  Develop and test models of heat flow around the walls, as well as implement them for routine use;  Develop and test new approaches for geotechnical design for energy retaining walls.    As a Research Fellow in Energy Geostructures on this project you will lead research in delivering new knowledge on the thermal design and performance of energy walls to facilitate rapid implementation of embedded retaining walls for widespread application. You will:    Undertake numerical simulations of energy walls, and understand which modelling and ground condition simplifications are acceptable with reference to field data as appropriate;  Develop, test and implement analytical models for planar heat flow around energy walls;  Work closely with project partners at University of Sao Paolo and University of Dundee to integrate their inputs and outputs into your analysis;  Collaborate with other University of Leeds researchers on development of energy systems modelling tools for energy walls;  Take a leading role in production of project outputs including journal papers and accessible guidance for practice. We are seeking a highly motivated Post-Doctoral Research Fellow to join the research group of Professor Laura Carter, UKRI Future Leaders Fellow, and contribute to the pioneering UK Research and Innovation-funded project, Closing the Loop: Emerging Contaminants in Agricultural Environments.  Sustainable agricultural practices, including the use of treated wastewater for irrigation and organic waste-derived soil amendments, are increasingly being adopted to address global challenges such as water scarcity and the need to reduce reliance on synthetic fertilisers. items.title: Fully funded PhD place at ISEY - Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth at UEL (PHD004-26)
items.description:
Fully funded PhD place at ISEY - Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth at UEL   “Reading Together: Interpersonal Neural Mechanisms of Learning in Caregiver-Child Interactions”  *Unfortunately, we cannot accept international applications, unless self-funded, for this PhD     The Project   A funded PhD position is available to address a fundamental question in developmental science: how does shared reading between caregivers and young children support early learning, and what are the interpersonal neural mechanisms that underpin these benefits? Shared reading is one of the strongest predictors of children's early language, literacy and cognitive development. Through shared books, children are exposed to new vocabulary, more complex language structures, as well as reciprocal interactions with adults. Experimental research has shown that interventions promoting caregiver-child book sharing can improve children's subsequent language outcome and attention skills.   Shared reading is a dynamic, interactive process. Caregivers continuously adapt their speech, gaze, gestures and pacing in response to children's attention and behaviour. These moment-to-moment adjustments may create optimal opportunities for learning by helping children attend to, process and retain new information. The temporal coordination of adult behaviour and infant’s neural activity may therefore be a key mechanism through which shared reading supports development.  Currently, however, we understand very little about how learning unfolds moment-to-moment during these interactions, and how underlying neural mechanisms support later developmental outcomes.  The PhD project aims to move beyond quantity-based measures of shared reading to investigate the neural mechanisms through which caregiver-child interactions support learning. By addressing the following questions:   How do caregivers and children coordinate their behaviour during shared reading, and which features of this interaction create optimal opportunities for learning?  How does moment-to-moment neural activity, measured using dual-brain EEG, become coordinated between caregivers and children during shared reading?  How does interpersonal neural coordination relate to children's attention, engagement and learning during shared reading?  How do the timing and quality of shared reading interactions predict children's subsequent learning and developmental outcomes?   By integrating measures of behaviour, attention and dual-brain neural activity, the project will provide a mechanistic account of how shared reading supports early learning. Combining state-of-the-art caregiver-child EEG recordings with fine-grained measures of interaction will help reveal how learning emerges through real-time coordination between two people, providing new insights into the processes through which early shared experiences shape children's development.     The University and ISEY   The PhD will be based at The Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth ISEY, at the Stratford Campus of The University of East London. This research institute is led by Prof. Sam Wass, and the PhD will be supervised by Dr Ira Marriott Haresign. The successful candidate would be working within a wider team of 20 researchers at ISEY.  Knowledge exchange and dissemination will be a key part of this PhD and the successful candidate will be expected to share project findings and associated research with teachers and early years practitioners, as part of the  training and development services  that ISEY offers. Therefore, this role is especially suitable for someone passionate about bridging the gap between research and practice and translating research for a non-scientific audience. This may involve writing articles for educator-facing publications, attending early years events and running online and face to face training, support will be given in these areas.      The applicant  Experience  The PhD candidate must have a first or upper second-class undergraduate honours degree and preferably a Masters in a discipline relevant to the project. While we expect that this project would suit graduates from a psychology background, we are happy to receive applications from a range of backgrounds that have potential to enhance the project (e.g. computer science, education psychology, media analysis...)    Experience working with children is highly desirable.   Familiarity with programming and data analysis tools is also preferable as the PhD will involve advanced quantitative data analysis, although support will be given in this area.   Successful applicants should have an interest in auditory or visual attention, speech and language processing, arousal, and EEG.  Methods   The successful candidates will also potentially use our custom-built wearable devices and be willing to analyse multi-streamed timeseries (physiological and behavioural day-long recordings).   Familiarity with eye-tracking and EEG is also highly desirable, as is experience with associated data analysis tools.   ISEY also has a newly developed virtual reality and motion tracking lab and this project may also consider the use of these methods to address the research questions.   Whilst some remote work is possible, the successful candidate will need to be willing to be based at the ISEY lab, in Stratford, London for at least 50% of the time. During data collection periods PhD students may need to be in London every day.   Please note that we are drawing all applicants’ attention to the fact that unfortunately, the funding available for this project does not cover the higher tuition fees required for international students. As a result, we are only able to consider applicants who would be classified as UK/home students (including UK nationals and those with settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme).  If you are an international student, I’m afraid we will be unable to proceed with your application unless you are self-funding.       How to apply  Applications must be submitted by email to  I.Marriott-haresign@uel.ac.uk  by the 20th November 2026. Interviews are likely to take place in December.    Please send your CV along with the names and contact details of two referees who will be contacted directly. At least one of the references must be academic.   Please also include a personal statement/cover letter (no more than 1000 words) which demonstrates your motivation and readiness for undertaking a PhD and for this specific PhD project.   Funding details and start dates  The PhD can start in January 2027.   Funding covers tuition fees (approx £5-8k per year) and a stipend set at the ESRC/UKRI rate for London Universities (£22,780 p.a) if studying full time. Part time study is based on 0.6FTE and the stipend will be adjusted accordingly (£13,668), lasting for up to 5 years.
